input.question: How do hospitals dispose of donated blood/organs that go bad and can't be used anymore?
input.ground_truth: In some cases they don't. Back when I was a nuclear medicine intern I once saw an entire fridge filled with radioactive livers, some of which were many years old. The patients had been given radioactive medicine to help cure liver cancer, and in the cases when it didn't work and the patient died, they would have to remove the liver for safety reasons. Instead of spending the money to properly dispose of the radioactive waste (very expensive) the hospital just dumped them in an old fridge in the basement. This was at one of the top 10 hospitals in the US btw, not just some sketchy clinic.

Okay! Imagine you have a special box where you keep juice boxes. But sometimes, the juice gets old and you can’t drink it because it’s not good anymore.

Hospitals have a special place too, but instead of juice, they keep blood or organs to help sick people. But if the blood or organ gets too old and can’t help anyone, they can’t use it.

So, what do they do? They throw it away in a very safe and careful way! They put it in special bags or containers so nobody gets hurt, and they make sure it’s cleaned up really well, just like how you have to throw away old milk carefully so it doesn’t make a mess or smell bad.

They don’t just throw it in the trash. They follow special rules to keep everyone safe and the world clean.
